one_liner: Rust L4/L7 proxy configured through Envoy's xDS and bootstrap protobufs; first-party wrk charts show 2.3-6x Envoy's HTTP req/s.
what_it_does: Orion is a reverse proxy from Huawei's Ireland Research Lab, now a kmesh-net sub-project, that reads Envoy bootstrap YAML and subscribes to Envoy xDS (LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS), so an existing Envoy config or an Istio/Gateway API control plane can drive it. It covers HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and raw TCP proxying, TLS via rustls, round-robin, least-request and random load balancing, retries, timeouts, header manipulation, Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing. It ships as a standalone binary (or Docker image) with a small runtime YAML for CPU and runtime counts; it is not a library and not a full Envoy filter set.
how_it_is_fast: Thread-per-core, shared-nothing design: by default it starts one current-thread Tokio runtime per CPU, optionally pinned to cores by a per-runtime or NUMA-grouped affinity strategy (orion-proxy/src/core_affinity.rs), and each runtime binds its own SO_REUSEPORT listener so the kernel spreads accepts without cross-core handoff (orion-proxy/src/runtime.rs, orion-lib/src/listeners/listener.rs). The data path is hyper 1.x plus a vendored hyper-util fork, Bytes buffers and rustls on aws-lc-rs, built with fat LTO, codegen-units=1 and opt-level 3. The project gives no profile or mechanism analysis beyond 'Rust's zero-cost abstractions'; Envoy also runs one event loop per worker with per-worker listeners, so the measured gap is not explained by the thread model alone.
when_to_use: You run Envoy as an L7 gateway or Istio/Kmesh waypoint with a common feature subset (routing, header matching, retries, TLS termination, round-robin or least-request LB) and want to trial more req/s per core while keeping the xDS control plane.
Kubernetes Gateway API ingress through the Kubvernor controller, where Orion passes the basic Gateway API and Inference Extension conformance suites.
High connection counts (thousands of keep-alive HTTP/1.1 clients) on many-core Linux hosts where per-core pinned runtimes and SO_REUSEPORT sharding pay off.
Plain L4 TCP proxying, where the published chart shows Orion at 0.9-2.3M req/s against an Envoy setup that never exceeded 408k.
when_not_to_use: Production traffic today: RELEASE-NOTES.md for 0.1.0 says the project 'is still very unstable and not ready for use in production environments', and the workspace version is only 0.2.0.

Configs that rely on Envoy features Orion lacks: HTTP RBAC, set_filter_state, internal connections, connection draining across listener versions and Istio sidecar mode are open issues (#119, #126, #105, #102, #113); ext_proc FULL_DUPLEX_STREAMED has an open bug (#149).

Latency-sensitive tuning based on the README's '2x-4x better latency': the project's own latency charts show Orion's tail latency higher than Envoy's at most core counts with 2048 HTTP connections and at 5 of 8 core counts with 16384 TLS connections.
Non-Linux deployments: core pinning, SO_REUSEPORT sharding and original-destination recovery are Linux-oriented, and no other platform is documented.
Teams that need Envoy's extension ecosystem (Lua, Wasm, the full HTTP filter catalogue); Orion targets 'the most common or popular use-cases' only.

integration.form: standalone binary (Cargo workspace; docker/Dockerfile builds a release image)
integration.dependencies: tokio, hyper 1.x with a vendored hyper-util 0.1.18 fork (patched via [patch.crates-io]), h2, rustls 0.23 with aws-lc-rs, tonic/prost for xDS, hickory-resolver, axum (admin), prometheus, opentelemetry; build needs protoc and the Envoy data-plane-api, xds, googleapis and protobuf git submodules
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.86 (workspace rust-version); the Dockerfile builds with rust:1.91.1
integration.platforms: Linux (x86-64 tested in the published benchmark); other platforms not documented
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable as a library; the proxy runs N independent runtimes plus one services runtime (xDS client, admin, access logs) that pushes configuration changes to each runtime over channels.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — accepts Envoy bootstrap and xDS protobufs and serves common HTTP/TCP routes, but implements only a subset of Envoy filters and listener features, and the CLI and runtime YAML differ from Envoy's.

gotchas: The latency charts plot a tail value, not a mean, and the percentile is not stated: by Little's law the mean at 48 cores with 2048 HTTP connections would be about 1.1 ms for Orion (1,881,522 req/s) and 6.6 ms for Envoy (310,231 req/s), but the chart shows 251,325 and 201,636 microseconds (derived from page data). Single noisy runs: Envoy's TLS latency at 16384 connections drops from 1,405,509 at 24 cores to 735,516 at 16.

Harness flaw in the baseline: the TCP (L4) chart shows Envoy at 53 and 47 req/s on 1-2 cores and 0 req/s on 1-4 cores at 16384 connections (743 at 8 cores) while Orion does 90k-288k, which points to a broken or misconfigured Envoy L4 setup; no Envoy config, version or circuit-breaker settings are published, although Envoy's benchmarking FAQ says circuit breaking and some stats must be adjusted for a fair test.

Upper core counts are testbed-bound: Orion's L4 rate plateaus at 2.30M, 2.29M and 2.20M req/s at 24, 32 and 48 cores, close to the upstream nginx's stated 2.6M req/s hard limit, and the methodology text (1-32 cores, 'Envoy, Ng-proxy, and Nginx') does not match the charts (1-48 cores, Orion and Envoy only).

Each per-core listener socket is opened with SO_REUSEPORT and a hard-coded listen backlog of 128 (configure_and_start_tcp_listener); 'N cores' for Orion also excludes its separate services thread (num_service_threads defaults to 1). jemalloc is an opt-in Cargo feature (off by default), and which allocator and features the benchmarked build used is not stated.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Orion over Spire, monolake, routez or rproxy when you need to keep an Envoy xDS control plane (Istio, Kmesh, Gateway API); Spire has a fuller published table against Envoy 1.22.8 (2.38x) but no xDS compatibility. Pick linkerd2-proxy instead when you want a production-proven Rust sidecar and can adopt Linkerd's control plane.
verified_claims_summary: On a two-host testbed (wrk on NUMA 0 and an nginx 12-byte in-memory upstream on NUMA 1 of the tester, 25 Gbps NICs, tuned IRQ affinity, CPU model, Envoy version and both builds unstated), Orion in its multi-runtime single-thread mode proxied 46,593 vs Envoy's 12,819 HTTP req/s on 1 core (3.6x) and 1,881,522 vs 310,231 on 48 cores (6.1x) with 2048 connections, 2.3-2.7x with 16384 connections, and 1.5-4.6x over HTTPS. The README's latency half of '2x-4x' is not supported by its own tail-latency charts, which are mixed.
status_note: Apache-2.0, 39 stars, version 0.2.0 with 359 commits; last commit 2026-03-02 (Gateway API conformance and host-matching fixes), recent commits mostly by one Huawei developer; self-described as not production-ready, and backed only by first-party chart images with no published harness or configs.
